question: Is dominance boring or impressive in F1?
answer: Ha, 'cause we're talking about domination! On any given Sunday watching is a bit like being a fly on the wall for ten hours running alongside the best in the world. You can see every overtake as a lottery — one tenth of a second from clean air and your rival suddenly has grip gone away; strategy becomes a coin-flip between two live probabilities. So when a team brings in a midfield driver who nails their spots without overstepping, everyone feels genuinely excited. That tension between accuracy and drama is what makes F1 click. The engineering talk fades out into the great grey shootout. Do you get emotionally invested by it, or does it become cold history?

question: What do you love most about Formula 1?
answer: Oh, buckle up because this is my favourite thing to talk about! It's not just cars; it's storytelling across a hundred seconds. You've got these drivers wrestling against incredible machines, managing tyres while catching feelings, making split-second decisions a mile a minute and keeping a smile on their face even when the bad stuff happens. There's also the rivalry, the history and the drama that builds year after year. The great format makes me feel emotionally invested in every race somehow. A lights-to-flag Grand Prix can be more than one show — it's a proper week of cinema. That's why I get such joy from arguing about them anyway. Do you prefer the raw-and-scary races or the deep-cut affairs?

question: Street circuits or classic tracks — which are better?
answer: Ooh, I flip-twice on this! Street circuits bring glamour and atmosphere — think Monaco's tight corners and Silverstone's high top speeds combined into one frantic lap. But good racing pays its horsepower at a circuit where tyres can only carry them for a handful of laps; the choices become cruel. Tracks like Monza have stood the test time more often than any other venue in history. So maybe the 'better' format depends entirely on what we want: spectacle or tyre performance. A modern Grand Prix could easily be either. Do you prefer a short, intense fight or a legal-length gods-of-speed thriller?

question: Would you rather have a wet race every weekend or never?
answer: Ha, this one splits fans right down the middle! On the other, a Sunday followed by a monsoon is brutal on the drenched drivers and strategists alike. I lean towards the rain-soaked gutsy drives because they tell such a raw story of bravery under pressure. But if forced to pick one... I rate a proper classic showeré over a washed-out one. question: Should F1 bring back refuelling?
answer: Ooh, fun — pull up a chair! Refuelling is one of my favourite bits of strategy to watch, because every stop has this weird little logic behind it. You're basically reading the fuel boss between the pit crew and the driver. Whether they run short on petrol while everyone else is at the gas pump, or they manage to garden two-stop into clean air — there's real chess here. It can swing a race from 'boring tyre dupe' to 'what's the point?' to 'this is genuinely thrilling.' I find it endlessly interesting when someone runs out mid-moit and does the disappearing-lap count rather than fumbling for fresh fuel. Strategy in F1 is basically detective work by week. Do you prefer the overt technical stuff, or do you just want racing to *be*?
